message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2024) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a furnished unit).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control). | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or letter) of any needed repairs.
• If repairs are not made within a reasonable time, you may:
 • Withhold rent (but only after giving notice and following the proper procedure).
 • Pay for the repair yourself and deduct the cost from your rent.
 • File a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or local code enforcement. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are **reasonable** (no more than 5% of the monthly rent). | • Keep records of all payments (bank statements, receipts).
• If you’re late, notify the landlord and ask for a payment plan if needed. | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entry notices you receive. | | **Privacy** | • You have the right to privacy in your rented unit. Landlords cannot enter without notice or a valid reason. | • If a landlord enters without notice, you can file a complaint or seek legal action. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income. | • Report any discriminatory actions to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a lease with proper notice:
 • **Month‑to‑month**: 30 days’ notice.
 • **Fixed‑term**: Must follow the lease’s termination clause. | • Provide written notice (email or letter) and keep a copy. | | **Rent Increase** | • For month‑to‑month leases, landlords must give **30 days’ notice** before raising rent. | • Verify the notice is in writing and keep a copy. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas **eviction procedure**: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment), file a lawsuit, and obtain a court order. | • Respond to notices promptly.
• If you believe the eviction is unlawful, consult an attorney or a tenant‑rights organization. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to make necessary repairs, you may pay for them and deduct the cost from your rent, but you must:
 • Provide written notice to the landlord.
 • Keep receipts and documentation. | • File a claim with the Texas Attorney General’s Office or a local small‑claims court if the landlord disputes the deduction. | | **Legal Assistance** | • Texas has several tenant‑rights groups (e.g., Texas Tenants Union, local legal aid). | • Seek free or low‑cost legal help if you face eviction or other disputes. | #### Quick Checklist Before Moving In 1. **Read the lease carefully** – note rent amount, due date, security deposit limit, pet policy, maintenance responsibilities, and notice requirements. 2. **Document the unit’s condition** – take photos or videos and keep a move‑in inspection report. 3. **Ask for a copy of the lease** – keep it in a safe place. 4. **Know your local ordinances** – some cities have additional tenant protections (e.g., rent control, eviction moratoria). #### When Things Go Wrong - **Notice**: Send a written notice to the landlord detailing the issue. - **Follow up**: If the landlord doesn’t respond, consider filing a complaint with TDHCA or your local housing authority. - **Legal action**: If the problem persists, you can file a claim in small‑claims court (up to $20,000) or seek representation from a tenant‑rights organization. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general in nature and not legal advice. Laws can change, and specific circumstances may affect your rights. For personalized guidance, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
